rationale: B wins because it keeps the knife on the fact pattern instead of decorating it. A's labor headline says "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone," which turns workload equivalence into vanished humans; that is how you get a correction, not a story. B's version, "It won't say how many people lost their jobs," preserves the uncertainty and makes the refusal the news. Same basic four angles, but B has cleaner reporter shape and fewer little acts of overreach.
gaps_in_A: "the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" overstates the supplied fact; 700 FTE-equivalent work is not proof that 700 people are gone.
"whether an AI should decide your Klarna payment dispute" assumes adjudication; the update only says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes.
"advocacy concerns surfacing now are likely to precede regulatory attention" invents a regulatory trajectory the update does not give you.
"Before this, AI-in-customer-service claims were largely vendor-produced" is an unsupported market claim, and it does not need to be there.
gaps_in_B: "a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" still leans too far; the update does not establish that the assistant rules on disputes.
"The reporter will write this story with or without Klarna" is PR bravado dressed as certainty. Cut it or prove it.
"The update is fresh" is a weaker why-now than using the IPO filing for the labor and investor angles.
"Next step: meanest-editor" is the wrong workflow label; after choosing and tightening one angle, this needs journalist-fit-check or source development, not another roast.
